goals: Describe the bell curve by its mean and SD
Convert values to z-scores and percentiles
why: Measurement errors, manufacturing tolerances, test scores and averages of many things are approximately normal. Six Sigma quality programmes, control charts and confidence intervals all rely on it.
explain: The **normal distribution** is the symmetric bell curve. It is completely described by two numbers: the **mean** μ (centre) and the **standard deviation** σ (width).
**68–95–99.7 rule**: about 68% of values fall within ±1σ of the mean, 95% within ±2σ and 99.7% within ±3σ.
A **z-score** says how many SDs a value lies from the mean: z = (x − μ) / σ. It lets you compare apples and oranges (an exam score vs a sprint time).
Why is it everywhere? When many small independent effects add up, the total tends to be normal. That is the Central Limit Theorem, covered next.

formula.plain: z-score = distance from the mean in units of standard deviations.

example.title: Bolt diameters on a production line
steps: Within ±2 SD ≈ 95% → about 5% of bolts are rejected
Tighten the process to SD 0.0133 mm → ±3 SD → only 0.3% rejected
example.result: Reducing variation, not moving the mean, is what cuts scrap. That is the core idea of Six Sigma.

mistakes: Assuming everything is normal: incomes, claim sizes and web traffic are heavily skewed.
Using the 68–95–99.7 rule on small samples or skewed data.
takeaways: Bell curve defined by μ and σ

practice.code:
from scipy.stats import norm
print(norm.cdf(2) - norm.cdf(-2))          # 0.954  share within ±2 SD
print(norm.cdf(184, loc=170, scale=7))     # height 184 cm → 97.7th percentile
